title: The plain (Luke 6:17–26)
hookLine: Luke's beatitudes: blessed are you poor, and woe to you who are rich
tomorrow: give, and it will be given

lines: NOT THE MOUNTAIN: A LEVEL PLACE.
ON THE SAME GROUND AS EVERYONE.
cards: In Matthew, the Beatitudes come from a mountain: Jesus goes up, sits down, and teaches. Luke tells it differently, starting with the ground.
After the night of prayer, Jesus comes down with the twelve and "stood in the plain." The Greek means a level place. Not above the crowd; on the same ground as everyone.

And the crowd is huge and mixed, from Judea and Jerusalem, and from the coast of Tyre and Sidon, outside Israel, pushing forward to touch him, because, Luke says, power was coming out of him and healing them all.
Then he looks at his disciples, and starts to speak.

teach.h: BLESSED BE YE: SPOKEN TO YOU.
teach.b: In the King James words: "Blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are ye that hunger now: for ye shall be filled. Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh." Three things.
First, Luke says you: blessed are you poor, spoken to the hungry and crying people in front of him. Second, the word now.
Hungry now, weeping now; this isn't the final word on their lives.
Third, Matthew has poor in spirit, and Luke simply ye poor. Christians read the two side by side.
Some stress actual poverty, as in the Catholic teaching sometimes called the preferential option for the poor; others stress the humble heart that knows it needs God.
Then Luke does something Matthew doesn't: he turns the blessings over, and on the other side are woes.
"But woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation. Woe unto you that are full! for ye shall hunger. Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep."
Four blessings, four woes, like a coin with two faces.

teach.h: THE WOES: ALAS, NOT A CURSE.
teach.b: Woe in Greek is ouai, a cry rather than a curse; some readers hear it as alas, a warning said with sorrow.

teach.h: BLESSED BE YE POOR: FOR YOURS IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.
teach.b: The blessed in Luke are the hungry and the grieving, the ones on level ground. And the comfortable are warned, sadly, that comfort can become all the reward there is.

how: Christians often read Luke's Sermon on the Plain alongside Matthew's Sermon on the Mount, and some churches and charities draw on Luke 6:20–21 in their work with the poor and hungry.

games.q: after a night of prayer on the mountain, you're about to teach a huge, mixed crowd. where do you stand?
o: stay up on the mountain where everyone can see.
come down and stand with them on a level place.
games.why: Luke says he came down and stood in the plain, on the same ground as the crowd, and spoke to the poor as "you."

practice: Picture your own neighborhood or commute, and ask who is hungry now, who is weeping now, who people step around: the man outside the grocery store, the coworker who's been quiet since the funeral.
Hold each face for a breath, and ask gently what it would mean to stand on level ground with them. If you pray, you can hold them before God; if you don't, simply see them.

wordCard.voice: The plain. In Luke, Jesus teaches the Beatitudes on a level place, speaking to the poor, the hungry and the weeping as you, and adding four woes.
